summary: The Senas, a family from Karnataka settled in Rarh in western Bengal, served the Palas until Vijaya Sena (1096–1159) won independence and drove the last Pala king out of Gauda. Under Ballala Sena and Lakshmana Sena they ruled almost all of Bengal and patronised Sanskrit learning. In 1203–04 Bakhtiyar Khalji's horsemen surprised the old king at Nadia; the Senas lost western and northern Bengal and held out in the east until about 1230.
details: The Sena family came from the Kannada-speaking south. Their own Deopara inscription describes the founder, Samanta Sena, as a Brahmakshatriya, a Brahmin family that had taken up the warrior's role, who had migrated from Karnataka. He settled in Rarh, in western Bengal, and is dated about 1070 to 1095. At first the family held a subordinate position under the Pala kings, who were then struggling with rebellion in their heartland of Varendra.

Samanta Sena's son Hemanta Sena took the next step. In 1095 he usurped power and styled himself king, ruling for about a year until 1096. The Pala kingdom was weak: Ramapala had only just recovered Varendra from the Kaivarta rebels and depended on the loyalty of local chiefs. Families such as the Senas could bargain their support for more freedom, and Hemanta's claim to royal status marked the Senas' rise from local lords to a ruling dynasty.

Hemanta's son Vijaya Sena succeeded in 1096 and ruled for about 62 years, until 1159. He inherited a subordinate position in Rarh under the Palas but won his independence in return for helping Ramapala. His marriage to a princess of the Sura family strengthened his hold on Rarh, and he was remembered as a friend of the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga of Odisha. Patiently, he turned a western Bengal lordship into a kingdom ready to challenge the Palas themselves.

Pala records run to Madanapala's eighth regnal year, 1152–53. Most probably soon afterwards, Vijaya Sena defeated him, and the Pala king fled; Vijaya Sena then took the throne of Gauda. His Deopara inscription, near Rajshahi, lists victories over Nanya of Mithila, Raghava, probably the Eastern Ganga king of Odisha, and others, and says his fleet sailed west up the Ganges. He ruled from Vijayapuri and Bikrampur (Vikramapura), and Bengal was now united under the Senas.

Vijaya Sena's son Ballala Sena ruled from about 1159 to 1179. He is credited with defeating Govindapala and so ending the Pala dynasty, and he may have completed the conquest of northern Bengal and taken Magadha and Mithila. Tradition gives his kingdom five provinces: Vanga, Varendra, Rarh, Mithila and Bagari. He married Ramadevi, a Western Chalukya princess from the Deccan. Later tradition links him to the system of Kulinism among Brahmins and Kayasthas, but historians doubt this.

The Sena kings presented themselves as champions of Brahminical Hinduism and Sanskrit learning, in contrast to the Buddhist Palas. Ballala Sena was himself an author. According to a Sena inscription he wrote the Danasagara, a treatise on religious gift-giving, in 1168, and in 1169 he began the Adbhutasagara, a work on omens, which was left unfinished. In old age he and his queen reportedly retired to the confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna, leaving his son Lakshmana Sena in charge.

Lakshmana Sena had fought for his grandfather and father against Gauda, Kamarupa, Kalinga and the Gahadavala king Jayachandra of Varanasi. As king from about 1179 to 1206 he carried the Sena kingdom into Odisha and possibly as far as Varanasi; a later Sena inscription credits him with victory pillars at Varanasi, Allahabad and on the southern seacoast. His court included the poets Jayadeva, Dhoyi and Sharana and the scholar Halayudha, and his era was used to date documents in Bengal and Bihar for centuries.

After the Ghurid victories in northern India, the Turkic commander Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji began raiding east of Varanasi in the late 1190s. By 1200 he had subjugated much of Bihar, the old Pala heartland west of the Sena kingdom. His attacks destroyed the Buddhist monastic universities of Odantapuri and Vikramashila, according to later accounts, though whether he also destroyed Nalanda is debated. With Bihar in Muslim hands, the road into Bengal lay open.

Having taken Bihar, Bakhtiyar Khalji struck at Nadia (Nabadwip), where the aged Lakshmana Sena was staying, in 1203–04. The fullest account, in the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri written by 1260, says he arrived with a band of horsemen and was at first taken for a horse dealer; it is said only 18 riders kept up with his rapid advance. The old king, surprised at his dinner, fled with his retainers to eastern Bengal. Nadia fell, and the Senas lost western Bengal almost without a battle.

Rather than stay at Nadia, Bakhtiyar Khalji moved north to Lakhnauti, the old capital of Gauda, and made it the seat of his government; the Ghurid conquest of Bengal is usually dated to 1205. Northern Bengal (Varendra) came under his rule. The Senas kept only the south and east, the region of Vanga, ruled from Bikrampur near modern Dhaka. Bengal was now divided between a Muslim state in the northwest and a Hindu Sena kingdom in the east.

Lakshmana Sena died around 1206, the same year Bakhtiyar Khalji was assassinated after a disastrous campaign toward Tibet. Lakshmana's sons continued Sena rule in southeastern Bengal, out of reach of the new Muslim rulers in the northwest. Vishvarupa Sena reigned from about 1206 to 1225, keeping the dynasty independent in the south and east of Bengal, far from Lakhnauti. Bikrampur, already a Sena capital, became the centre of the shrunken kingdom in the Ganges delta.

Keshava Sena, another son of Lakshmana Sena, followed Vishvarupa Sena around 1225 and reigned until about 1230. Like his brother he kept the Sena kingdom independent in southern and eastern Bengal. His copper-plate inscription is a key source: it credits his father and grandfather with victory pillars at Varanasi, Allahabad and the southern sea, recalling the dynasty's days of glory. The kingdom he ruled, however, was only the eastern part of the Bengal his family once held.

The Sena dynasty is usually said to end around 1230, after Keshava Sena. The Persian chronicle Tabaqat-i-Nasiri suggests that descendants of Lakshmana Sena still ruled somewhere in eastern Bengal as late as 1245 or even 1260. In the southeast a new Hindu family, the Deva dynasty, rose to power; its strongest king, Damodaradeva, ruled from about 1231 to 1243 around Comilla, Noakhali and Chittagong, and a later king took Bikrampur.
